title: Maya Chen Studio: freelancer deductions, self-employment tax and estimated payments
participant_role: Tax associate at a CPA firm advising a first-year freelance videographer on deductions, taxes and records
judge_role: Maya Chen, a sole proprietor videographer who earned $90,000, made no estimated payments and wants to deduct everything

difficulty.rationale: The Tax rules exhibit gives each rule (50% meals, Section 179, self-employment tax, due dates), so students apply the rules to the client's list instead of recalling them.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a tax associate at a CPA firm. Your client, MAYA CHEN (judge), is a freelance videographer who operates MAYA CHEN STUDIO as a sole proprietor. Maya Chen (judge) wants you to review her business expenses and help her understand what she owes and how to plan for next year.

Maya Chen (judge) has just finished her first full year as a freelancer. She films weddings, corporate events and social media content, and she received $90,000 in payments from clients during the year. Before going freelance, she worked as an employee and had taxes withheld from every paycheck, so she did not make any estimated tax payments this year.

Maya Chen (judge) brought you the list of "business expenses" shown below and said, "I spent all of this money because of my business, so I should be able to deduct all of it, right?" Your firm's summary of the tax rules that apply is also shown below. Your firm's tax software estimates that if she earns the same income next year, she will owe about $10,000 of self-employment tax and about $8,000 of federal income tax.

You must:
- Apply the tax rules to identify which of the listed items are deductible business expenses on Schedule C and explain why the others are not
- Calculate the net profit from the business
- Explain self-employment tax and plan the quarterly estimated tax payments for next year
- Recommend record keeping procedures for the business
- Explain your responsibilities as a tax professional

You will present your information to Maya Chen (judge) in a role-play to take place in your office at the CPA firm. Maya Chen (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your information and have answered Maya Chen's (judge's) questions, Maya Chen (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: My friend says I should form an LLC so I don't have to pay self-employment tax. Is that right?
What happens if I just pay everything in April?

solution.overview: A strong answer sorts the list into $19,000 of deductible Schedule C expenses and the personal or nondeductible items, arriving at net profit of $71,000. The presenter explains the 15.3% self-employment tax, sets up quarterly estimated payments of $4,500, recommends clear records, and makes it clear that a tax professional cannot deduct personal items even when the client asks.

answer: Deductible (ordinary and necessary for the business): camera $12,000 (Section 179 expensing), software $2,500, vehicle business portion $3,000, meals 50% = $500, home office $1,000
Total deductible expenses = $19,000
Not deductible: Hawaii vacation (personal, not business travel) and everyday clothing (suitable for everyday wear)
Traffic ticket: fines and penalties are never deductible
Health insurance: not a Schedule C expense, but it may qualify for the self-employed health insurance deduction on Form 1040
Net profit = gross receipts - deductible expenses
$90,000 - $19,000 = $71,000 net profit on Schedule C
Net profit is subject to both income tax and self-employment tax

by_task.task: Explain self-employment tax and plan the quarterly estimated tax payments for next year
answer: Self-employed people pay both the employee and employer shares of Social Security and Medicare: 15.3% on 92.35% of net profit (Schedule SE)
Example: $71,000 x 92.35% x 15.3% is about $10,000, matching the software estimate
Half of the self-employment tax is deductible on Form 1040
Estimated total for next year: $10,000 + $8,000 = $18,000, so $4,500 per quarter (Form 1040-ES)
Due dates: April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15; late or missing payments bring an underpayment penalty
Tip: move about 20% of each client payment into a separate tax savings account
Use a separate business bank account and credit card
Keep invoices, receipts and 1099 forms; scan them into a folder or app
Keep a mileage log as you drive (date, destination, business purpose, miles)
Write on each meal receipt who attended and the business purpose; keep home office measurements and photos
Keep records at least 3 years after filing, longer for equipment purchases
Prepare an accurate return with due diligence under IRS Circular 230 and AICPA standards
Do not deduct personal items even if the client asks; explain the rules instead
Keep client information confidential
Advise the client on penalties and planning so there are no surprises

calculations.label: Items not deductible on Schedule C
steps: Health insurance $4,800 (not on Schedule C; possible Form 1040 adjustment)
calculations.result: $10,050 of the list stays off Schedule C

judge_question_answers.question: My friend says I should form an LLC so I don't have to pay self-employment tax. Is that right?
answer: No: a single-member LLC is a disregarded entity for tax, so the profit still goes on Schedule C and is still subject to self-employment tax
An LLC does give legal liability protection, which may be worth it for a business with clients and equipment
Electing S corporation status could reduce self-employment tax if she pays herself a reasonable salary, but it adds payroll, a separate return and extra fees
Compare the savings to the added costs before deciding

judge_question_answers.question: What happens if I just pay everything in April?
answer: The IRS expects tax to be paid as income is earned, so waiting until April creates an underpayment penalty (interest-like charge for each late quarter)
Safe harbor: no penalty if payments equal 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's tax (110% if income is high)
Paying $4,500 each quarter avoids the penalty and a large bill all at once

key_concepts.definition: The IRS form a sole proprietor uses to report business income and expenses. Net profit = gross receipts - deductible business expenses.
An expense that is common in the business and helpful for earning income; only these business expenses are deductible, never personal costs.
An election that lets a business deduct the full cost of qualifying equipment in the year it is placed in service instead of depreciating it over several years.
Meals with clients for a business purpose are generally only 50% deductible. Deduction = meal cost x 50%.
A space used regularly and only for business can be deducted at $5 per square foot, up to 300 square feet. Deduction = square feet x $5.
Social Security and Medicare tax paid by self-employed people, covering both the employee and employer shares. SE tax = net profit x 92.35% x 15.3%; half is deductible on Form 1040.
Quarterly payments (Form 1040-ES) that self-employed people make because no tax is withheld. Quarterly payment = expected annual tax / 4.
A penalty charged when too little tax is paid during the year. It is avoided by paying at least 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's tax (110% for high incomes).
A deduction on Form 1040 (not Schedule C) for health insurance premiums paid by a self-employed person who is not eligible for an employer plan.
Keeping receipts, logs and tax records to support every deduction, generally for at least 3 years after filing and longer for asset purchases.
The Treasury rules that govern people who practice before the IRS, requiring due diligence, accuracy and honest advice to clients.

notes: State level because students must judge nine items against the rules in the Tax rules exhibit, explain self-employment tax, and plan payments while advising a client who wants every expense deducted. Watch for students who deduct 100% of meals, put health insurance on Schedule C, forget that fines are never deductible, or tell the judge an LLC eliminates self-employment tax.

items.label: Explain record keeping procedures for tax accounting

criteria.exceeds: Recommends a separate business bank account and credit card, scanned invoices, receipts and 1099 forms, a mileage log kept as she drives (date, destination, purpose, miles), notes on each meal receipt of who attended and why, home office measurements and photos, and keeping records at least 3 years (longer for equipment).
criteria.meets: Recommends a separate business account, keeping receipts and 1099 forms, a mileage log and meal documentation, and keeping records for at least 3 years.
criteria.below: Gives general advice such as "keep your receipts" without specific procedures for mileage, meals or the home office.
criteria.little: Does not recommend any record keeping procedures.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates net profit of $71,000, explains that self-employment tax is 15.3% of 92.35% of net profit (about $10,000, matching the software) because she pays both the employee and employer shares, notes half is deductible on Form 1040, and plans $18,000 of tax as four $4,500 payments due April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15.
criteria.meets: Calculates net profit of $71,000, explains self-employment tax, and plans quarterly estimated payments of $4,500 ($18,000 / 4) with the four due dates.
criteria.below: Gets only part of the calculation, for example plans payments for income tax only ($2,000 a quarter) or cannot explain what self-employment tax covers.
criteria.little: Does not calculate net profit or the estimated payments, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibits.

criteria.exceeds: Identifies each nondeductible item and why (Hawaii vacation is personal, everyday clothing, the $150 traffic ticket since fines are never deductible, half the meals), explains that the $4,800 health insurance belongs on Form 1040 rather than Schedule C, and flags that making no estimated payments creates an underpayment penalty.
criteria.meets: Correctly identifies the vacation, clothing and traffic ticket as nondeductible, treats health insurance as a Form 1040 item, and warns about missing estimated payments.
criteria.below: Identifies some nondeductible items but misses others, for example puts health insurance on Schedule C or deducts 100% of meals.
criteria.little: Agrees that all of the listed expenses are deductible, or identifies no tax issues.

items.label: Discuss the effect of tax laws and regulations on financial transactions

criteria.exceeds: Applies each rule to reach $19,000 of deductions (camera $12,000 under Section 179, software $2,500, vehicle $3,000, meals 50% = $500, home office 200 sq ft x $5 = $1,000) and explains that $10,050 of the list stays off Schedule C, which changes both income tax and self-employment tax.
criteria.meets: Applies the tax rules to arrive at deductible Schedule C expenses of $19,000 and net profit of $71,000.
criteria.below: Applies some rules correctly but reaches a wrong total, for example includes the full $1,000 of meals or the $4,800 of health insurance.
criteria.little: Does not apply the tax rules, or deducts the whole list.

items.label: Explain the responsibilities of finance professionals in providing client services

criteria.exceeds: Explains the duty to prepare an accurate return with due diligence under IRS Circular 230 and AICPA standards, to refuse to deduct personal items even when the client asks while explaining the rules, to keep client information confidential, and to advise on penalties and planning so there are no surprises.
criteria.meets: Explains that a tax professional must prepare an accurate return, cannot deduct personal items because the client asks, and must keep client information confidential.
criteria.below: Mentions honesty in general terms without connecting it to Maya's request to deduct everything.
criteria.little: Does not address professional responsibilities, or offers to deduct the personal items anyway.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects each deduction decision to net profit, self-employment tax, income tax and the quarterly payment plan, and checks that $71,000 x 92.35% x 15.3% is about $10,000.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the tax rules to the deductible total, net profit and payment plan.
criteria.below: Reaches conclusions without showing the reasoning, or misses how deductions affect the taxes owed.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives Maya a clear, practical plan: pay $4,500 each quarter, move about 20% of each client payment into a separate tax savings account, and set up records now for next year.
criteria.meets: Makes clear recommendations on which items to deduct and how to pay estimated taxes.

criteria.exceeds: Explains the tax rules and self-employment tax in plain language a new freelancer can follow, and tells her tactfully that several items are not deductible, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the deductions, net profit, taxes and record keeping clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on tax jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses an effective visual such as a two column list of deductible and nondeductible items or a payment calendar, and adds a useful idea such as a receipt scanning app or the 20% tax savings habit.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the deductions and payment plan easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or practical.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: a single-member LLC is a disregarded entity, so profit stays on Schedule C with self-employment tax, though it gives liability protection and an S corporation election could save tax at the cost of payroll and fees; and paying everything in April brings an underpayment penalty unless a safe harbor (90% of this year or 100% of last year) is met, so $4,500 a quarter is better.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that an LLC alone does not remove self-employment tax and that waiting until April causes an underpayment penalty.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without reasons.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says an LLC eliminates self-employment tax.

key_points: Deductible Schedule C expenses total $19,000: camera $12,000 (Section 179), software $2,500, vehicle $3,000, meals 50% = $500, home office 200 sq ft x $5 = $1,000
Not deductible on Schedule C: Hawaii vacation, everyday clothing, the $150 traffic ticket (fines never deductible) and half of meals; health insurance may be deducted on Form 1040
Self-employment tax is 15.3% of 92.35% of net profit (both employee and employer shares), about $10,000; half is deductible on Form 1040
Estimated payments: $10,000 + $8,000 = $18,000 / 4 = $4,500 due April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15
Records: separate business account, receipts and 1099 forms, mileage log, meal purpose notes, keep at least 3 years
A tax professional must prepare an accurate return and cannot deduct personal items even when the client asks
